attributes.nuance_translation: The negative form of a single-conjugation verb, in either its polite or casual variant.

attributes.body:
The negative form of る-Verbs are conjugated based on the same set of rules used for other forms of る-Verb conjugation (removal of る, followed by the addition of something else). In the case of negation, the additional component will be ない (casual), or ません (polite).

While the common translation of ない and ません is simply 'not', they actually have several possible nuances. These nuances are 'don't' (usually not), 'won't' (intentionally not), or 'can't' (unintentionally not).

Both ない and ません are auxiliary verbs (ません is a conjugation of ます), meaning that they have their own set of conjugation rules.

A semi-polite form may also be used. This is constructed by using ない, and then simply adding です. です is used to mark politeness here, and ないです sounds less formal and stiff than ません.

Caution

The ない attached to make the negative form of adjectives is a different word, and therefore follows different conjugation rules. When attached to adjectives ない itself is an い-Adjective, and not an auxiliary verb.

attributes.description: Negation of masu verbs ません
Informal Past Negative form of Verbs

attributes.body: These forms express the negative ('does not' or 'will not') of る-Verbs, with a difference in tense. The る-Verb (Negative) expresses a lack of future or habitual action (e.g., 食べない = 'I don't eat' or 'I won't eat'). The る-Verb (Negative-Past) expresses a lack of past action (e.g., 食べなかった = 'I didn't eat'). Both are plain forms used in casual speech or other grammatical patterns.

The past form of a verb expresses completed actions or past states, while the negative form expresses actions or states that do not occur. る-Verbs form their negative by changing る to ない (e.g., 食べる → 食べない), whereas う-Verbs form the past tense differently (e.g., 買う → 買った). Remember, not all verbs ending in る are る-Verbs, for example, 帰る ('to return') is an う-verb.

The negative form of a る-verb indicates 'does not' or 'will not' do something (e.g., 食べない = 'I don't eat' or 'I won't eat'). In contrast, じゃない (a casual form of ではない, the negative of だ) negates nouns and な-adjectives (e.g., 元気じゃない = 'not feeling good'). While both express negation, they apply to different types of words.

The negative form of a る-verb expresses that someone does not or will not perform an action (e.g., 食べない = 'I do not eat' or 'I will not eat'). The Verb + て form, on the other hand, connects verbs with other sentence elements, expressing sequences, requests, or permission. For example, 食べて can mean 'Eat, please' in a casual request.

The non-past (or dictionary) form is the base form of a verb, used to express habitual or future actions (e.g., 食べる = 'I eat' or 'I will eat'). To express the negative, use the negative form. For most える/いる-Verbs, change the final る to ない (e.g., 食べない = 'I do not eat' or 'I will not eat'). Both the non-past and negative forms are plain forms used in casual conversation or other grammar patterns.

The dictionary form is the base form of the verb, used for habitual or future actions. The negative form expresses that an action doesn't happen or a state doesn't exist. For る-Verbs, the negative is formed by changing る to ない (e.g., 食べる → 食べない). う-Verbs have different conjugation patterns. Be careful: not all verbs ending in る are る-Verbs—for example, 帰る ('to return') is actually an う-Verb.
